subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Study of a set drama text
Essay (whole-text) response on character, theme and dramatic method

questions.q: In drama, what is a soliloquy?
options: A speech delivered by a character alone on stage, revealing their inner thoughts
A short remark spoken to another character in confidence
A song performed by the chorus between scenes
A written instruction telling actors how to move
questions.explain: A soliloquy lets a solitary character voice private thoughts directly to the audience.

questions.q: What is an 'aside' in a play?
options: A brief remark spoken so the audience (or one character) hears it but others on stage do not
A lengthy speech given by a lone character
A description of the stage setting
The interval between two acts
questions.explain: An aside is a short comment heard by the audience but supposedly unheard by other characters.

questions.q: Dramatic irony occurs when:
options: The audience knows something important that one or more characters do not
A character says the opposite of what they mean for comic effect
The plot ends unexpectedly and unhappily
The playwright uses rhyme instead of prose
questions.explain: Dramatic irony arises from a gap between the audience's knowledge and a character's ignorance.

questions.q: What are stage directions?
options: Instructions in the text describing setting, actions, movement or delivery
The spoken lines exchanged between characters
The moral message of the play
The list of characters at the front of the text
questions.explain: Stage directions guide staging, movement and delivery rather than being spoken aloud.

questions.q: When analysing a printed extract, why might a candidate comment on the stage directions?
options: Because they shape mood, movement and how lines should be delivered on stage
Because they always rhyme with the dialogue
Because they replace the need to quote spoken lines
Because they reveal the examiner's preferred answer
questions.explain: Stage directions are a dramatic method that contributes to atmosphere and characterisation.

questions.q: How does a monologue differ from a soliloquy?
options: A monologue is a long speech that may be addressed to other characters present, not only to oneself
A monologue is always sung, while a soliloquy is spoken
A monologue is spoken only by the villain
A monologue is a stage direction, not speech
questions.explain: A monologue can be delivered to others on stage, whereas a soliloquy is spoken when alone.

questions.q: In a drama text, the protagonist is:
options: The central character around whom much of the action revolves
The character who opposes the hero
The narrator who introduces each scene
A minor character used for comic relief
questions.explain: The protagonist is the main character whose journey drives the play.

questions.q: The antagonist in a play is best described as:
options: The character or force in conflict with the protagonist
The character who speaks the prologue
The playwright's spokesperson
The character with the most soliloquies
questions.explain: The antagonist provides opposition and conflict for the protagonist.

questions.q: A tragedy is a dramatic form typically characterised by:
options: A serious plot leading to the downfall or suffering of the main character
A happy ending in which lovers are united
Everyday comic misunderstandings resolved cheerfully
A sequence of unconnected humorous sketches
questions.explain: Tragedy centres on serious conflict culminating in the protagonist's downfall or suffering.

questions.q: A passage-based (extract) question asks how the playwright makes a moment 'tense and dramatic'. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Analyse specific words, actions and dramatic methods within the given extract to show how tension is created
Summarise the whole plot of the play from beginning to end
Describe the biography of the playwright
Compare the play with an unrelated novel
questions.explain: Extract questions reward close analysis of the passage's language and dramatic methods.

questions.q: What most distinguishes a passage-based response from a whole-text essay?
options: It focuses closely on the detail of a specific printed extract
It forbids any reference to characters
It must be written entirely in verse
It requires learning the extract by heart
questions.explain: The passage-based task centres on detailed analysis of the given extract itself.

questions.q: A whole-text essay response typically requires candidates to:
options: Range across the play, using selected references to develop a sustained argument
Quote only from the final scene
Retell every event in chronological order
Focus on a single line of dialogue
questions.explain: Essay responses draw on the whole text, selecting evidence to support an argument.

questions.q: In literary study, a 'theme' is:
options: A central idea or message explored throughout a text
A single character's name
The rhyme scheme of a speech
The physical setting of the opening scene
questions.explain: A theme is a recurring idea or concern developed across the work.

questions.q: An extract reads: '[He turns away, his hands trembling.]' What kind of dramatic method is this, and what might a candidate say about it?
options: A stage direction that conveys the character's fear or agitation through physical action
A soliloquy revealing the character's plans
Dramatic irony directed at the audience
A rhyming couplet closing the scene
questions.explain: The bracketed instruction is a stage direction whose physical detail signals inner emotion.

questions.q: 'Characterisation' refers to:
options: The methods a playwright uses to create and develop characters
The number of actors in a production
The order in which scenes are performed
The historical period in which a play is set
questions.explain: Characterisation covers the techniques used to build and reveal characters.

questions.q: The 'denouement' of a play is:
options: The final part in which the plot is resolved and loose ends are tied up
The opening that introduces the setting and characters
The point of greatest tension
A humorous subplot
questions.explain: The denouement is the resolution following the climax.

questions.q: Foreshadowing is a dramatic technique in which:
options: Earlier details hint at events that will happen later in the play
A character speaks directly to the audience
The setting is described in detail
Two characters argue on stage
questions.explain: Foreshadowing plants clues that anticipate later developments.

questions.q: An essay question asks: 'How does the playwright present the relationship between two characters?' The strongest answer will:
options: Analyse the playwright's dramatic methods and use evidence from across the play to explore the relationship
List every scene the two characters appear in without analysis
Discuss only the candidate's personal opinion of the characters
Describe the costumes worn in a stage production
questions.explain: 'How does the playwright present' signals analysis of methods with whole-text evidence.

questions.q: In an extract, a character reassures another that 'all is well', but the audience has just seen the danger approaching. A close analysis should identify this as:
options: Dramatic irony that heightens tension for the audience
A soliloquy expressing private thoughts
An aside to a third character
A stage direction describing movement
questions.explain: The audience's superior knowledge of the danger makes the reassurance dramatically ironic.

questions.q: The 'exposition' of a play mainly functions to:
options: Introduce characters, setting and background needed to understand the action
Bring the plot to its most intense moment
Resolve the central conflict
Provide comic relief before the ending
questions.explain: Exposition supplies the background information that establishes the drama.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Literature in English (0475) syllabus; Paper 2: Drama
